newsitem.title: USA: Intel CFO reiterates Q1 margin on track.
newsitem.headline: Intel CFO reiterates Q1 margin on track.

text.p: Intel Corp's chief financial officer Andy Bryant said first quarter business remains on track with previously stated expectations and reiterated that first quarter gross profit margins would equal or fall below the fourth quarter's percentage of 62.9 percent.

"Q1... is exactly the same as what I told you it was at the beginning of the quarter," Bryant said of guidance Intel provided in its fourth quarter earnings report last month. He noted that Intel is meeting its monthly performance goals, saying that, "What's happened to date has been right on those monthly goals."
The Intel executive made the comments to money managers at the Goldman Sachs Technology Symposium here Tuesday.
Bryant added that Intel remains comfortable with its previously stated expectations of 60 percent plus growth in gross margin percentage terms.
In his presentation, Bryant sought to reassure jittery investors that the blue-chip technology issue's long term growth prospects remain strong.

Looking forward, he pointed to a recent Dataquest market projection that shows personal computer units worldwide growing at 17 percent in compound annual percentage terms through the year 2000. Intel makes roughly 90 percent of the microprocessor chips that serve as the brains of personal computers.

While declining to make a specific projection on the chipmaker's revenue growth expectations in the coming years, Bryant said, "These are the (market research figures) we are looking at" of Dataquest's 17 percent annual growth estimate.
He then added, "Seventeen percent to the end of the decade happens to match pretty closely what happened in the last decade."
Bryant said Intel focuses on boosting the absolute dollar amount of gross margins each quarter, and that percentage margin was a function of the particular mix of products in any particular period.

"We manage the company to bring those dollars up," Bryant said, referring to absolute gross margin dollars, or total revenues minus operating expenses. "We will accept a range of results as long as absolute gross margins go up," he said.
"We don't worry much about the percentage. We will do all we can to (acheive) the absolute dollar growth," he added.
He reiterated the company's long-term projection that gross margins in the future may return to a more sustainable range of 50 percent, but offered no timeline for when this might transpire.

Bryant said the company continues to be an ongoing buyer of its stock. He noted that at current rates the current share buyback authorization would have to be renewed before the end of the first half of 1997.

Bryant noted that Intel's fourth quarter gross margin of 62.9 percent was artificially high due to the company's decision to forego its traditional round of quarterly product price cuts in November, even as fixed costs remained roughly even. For 1996 as a whole, gross margins stood around 56 percent, by contrast.
